extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, reporters, and general readers interested in newswriting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing a news lead that contains the essential factual elements of a story by answering the fundamental questions (the Five Ws and related H). Useful for writing leads, press releases, and planning interviews or research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five Ws (overall checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Five Ws is a checklist used in journalism to ensure that the lead contains all the essential points of a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters were taught that the lead should answer these questions about the situation being reported: Who? What? Where? Why? When? The Five Ws are also used to guide research and interviews and to raise important ethical questions (for example, 'How do you know that?').

rubrics_metrics.name: Who
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify who is/was involved in the event or action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answering 'Who?' specifies the person(s) or entities responsible, affected, or central to the story — a fundamental element to place actors in the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: What
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe what happened or what the story is about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'What?' captures the action, event, fact, or issue being reported; it is the core factual element of the lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where
rubrics_metrics.description: State the location where the event occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Where?' situates the story geographically — the place or setting that is relevant to understanding the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: When
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify the time when the event occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'When?' establishes the timing or chronology, which can affect newsworthiness and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the reasons or motives behind the event or action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Why?' addresses cause, purpose, or motive; historically treated as one of the most important circumstances for explaining action.

rubrics_metrics.name: How (in what way)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the manner or method by which something happened ('in what way').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often appended as the H to the Five Ws ('Five Ws and one H'); covers the manner, method, or process (e.g., gently or violently) and helps distinguish voluntary from involuntary action in some analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: With / By what means (instrument/faculty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify instruments, aids, or means used ('with what').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical formulations include an element for 'with' or 'by what auxiliaries' (quibus auxiliis) — useful for specifying tools, resources, or accomplices relevant to the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use beyond the lead: research, interviews and ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Five Ws are used not only to craft leads but also to guide research and interviews and to surface ethical questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists use the questions to plan reporting and to probe sources (e.g., 'How do you know that?'); educators and other professions (data analytics, military orders) also adopt the framework to identify context and requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic caution: do not mechanically cram all Five Ws into the first sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: By mid-20th century critics described forcing all Five Ws into the first sentence as 'old-fashioned and fallacious.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes that the 'old-fashioned lead of the five Ws and the H' has been giving way to 'the much more supple and interesting feature lead.' Apply the Five Ws flexibly — prioritize readability and storytelling rather than rigidly packing every W into the opening sentence.
